extracted.intended_audience: students and researchers in probability, statistics, and philosophy of science
extracted.subtask_description: Principles for estimating probabilities and deciding when observed conjunctions of phenomena justify inferring causal laws rather than chance. Covers Laplace's classical definition, Bayesian (antecedent×likelihood) reasoning, and limits of empirical induction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's classical definition of probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The theory of chances consists in reducing all events of the same kind to a certain number of cases equally possible ... The ratio of that number [favorable cases] to the number of all the possible cases is the measure of the probability; which is thus a fraction, having for its numerator the number of cases favorable to the event, and for its denominator the number of all the cases which are possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Requires that (a) among the events one, and only one, must happen, and (b) we have no grounds to expect any one rather than another (equally undecided). Illustrated by coins and dice; used when events can be reduced to equally possible cases.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requisites for applying the calculus of chances
rubrics_metrics.description: To a calculation of chances ... two things are necessary; we must know that of several events some one will certainly happen, and no more than one; and we must not know, nor have any reason to expect, that it will be one of these events rather than another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes contention that mere ignorance is insufficient—experience showing equal frequency or deductive knowledge (e.g., mechanical symmetry) may be required to justify equal probabilities. Use caution: confirm the premises before applying simple counting methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Probability as degree of belief given evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of an event is not a quality of the event itself, but a mere name for the degree of ground which we ... have for expecting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability is subjective to the evidential state: different observers or the same observer with new evidence will assign different probabilities (example: learning a person is in the last stage of consumption changes death probability). Do not conflate event-objective certainty with epistemic probability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principle of insufficient reason / indifference (practical betting rule)
rubrics_metrics.description: When we know nothing of the proportion in which possibilities are mixed, we may reasonably judge them equally probable and act accordingly (e.g., bet with equal indifference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by balls-in-a-box examples. When three colors are possible and proportions unknown, logical symmetry can create computable odds (e.g., probability two-to-one against one color). But this is a pragmatic rule for action under ignorance; seek specific knowledge when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer causal knowledge to raw frequency when estimating probability
rubrics_metrics.description: The probability of events, as calculated from their mere frequency in past experience, affords a less secure basis ... than their probability as deduced from an equally accurate knowledge of the frequency of occurrence of their causes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where possible, ascend to causes and estimate comparative frequencies of causes favorable/unfavorable to the event. Example: differing ball sizes change drawing probability; cause-based estimates correct empirical ratios. When causes cannot be observed, frequencies of effects must be used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improve data quality before complex calculation
rubrics_metrics.description: A very slight improvement in the data, by better observations, or by taking into fuller consideration the special circumstances of the case, is of more use than the most elaborate application of the calculus to probabilities founded on the data in their previous state of inferiority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warning against misapplications of probability calculus (e.g., to witness credibility or jury verdicts) where averages are poor guides for single cases. Prefer obtaining better observations and case-specific information rather than over-relying on crude averages/formulae.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace's Sixth Principle (probability of causes — antecedent × likelihood)
rubrics_metrics.description: Given an effect M and several possible causes, the probability that the effect was produced by any one cause is as the antecedent probability of the cause multiplied by the probability that the cause, if it existed, would have produced the given effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases I–III illustrate: when causes differ in antecedent frequency, or in conditional production rates, or both, the posterior odds are proportional to the product of antecedent odds and likelihood ratios. This is the basis for reasoning from effects to causes (Bayesian updating).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguishing casual coincidence from causal law via expected frequency
rubrics_metrics.description: If the number of instances in which a coincidence is observed, over and above that which would arise on the average from the mere concurrence of chances, is such that so great an amount of coincidences from accident alone would be an extremely uncommon event; we have reason to conclude that the coincidence is the effect of causation, and may be received ... as an empirical law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Compute probability of observed series under chance (e.g., 1/m^n). If that is extremely small, prefer the hypothesis of non-accidental cause—especially if the alternative (a law) would certainly produce the series. But estimating the antecedent probability of an unknown law is generally impossible; repeatability and experimental replication strengthen inference.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of estimating the probability of an unknown law
rubrics_metrics.description: When the coincidence cannot be accounted for by any known cause and would imply an undiscovered law, the antecedent probability of that supposition is unsusceptible of approximate valuation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because we cannot plausibly estimate what fraction of natural sequences are law-governed versus casual, precise numerical comparison between chance and law hypotheses is impossible in such cases. Practical decisions rely on whether observed deviations are extremely unlikely under chance and on further investigation/replication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Induction is the foundation of probability calculations
rubrics_metrics.description: Such calculation of chances is grounded on an induction; and to render the calculation legitimate, the induction must be a valid one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Probability fractions reflect the ascertained proportion between cases in which the event occurs and all cases. The legitimacy of probabilistic inference depends on valid induction (representative sampling, stable conditions). Actuarial examples (life tables, hospital returns) show when frequency-based induction is used.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derivative empirical laws have limited generality and are collocation-dependent
rubrics_metrics.description: Derivative uniformities (laws of co-existence or sequence derived from causes) are less general than ultimate laws and often only obtain where there exists the same collocation of primeval causes; they are admissible only within the conditions of time and place confirmed by actual observation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not uncritically extend derivative empirical laws beyond observed collocations; counteracting causes or changed conditions can frustrate derivative regularities even when ultimate causal laws hold. Example: day and night on Earth depend on particular collocations (single sun + rotation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use probability to guide conduct under uncertainty, but seek better knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: Even when we have no knowledge except that some one of a certain number of possibilities must occur, we may still reasonably judge, and act conformably to, comparative probabilities derived from logical symmetry or minimal information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When stakes require action (betting decision or policy), act on the best available rational probability (even from indifference), but always endeavour to obtain better, specific data since slight information gains can materially change warranted probabilities.
